target_customer: Cargo operators and aerospace manufacturers wanting efficient electric aircraft, plus defence and maritime users of its drones
problem: First generation electric aircraft are heavy and have limited range and payload, creating a green penalty compared with conventional cargo aircraft.
business_model: Aircraft and drone product sales plus licensing of aerodynamic flow control technology to aerospace partners, funded largely by government grants so far
product_category: Aerospace hardware: electric cargo drones and aerodynamic flow control

founders.name: Graham Doig
prior_employers: Canoo (led aero and range team through its SPAC)
founders.background_notes: YC page: Lockheed Martin endowed engineering professor, over 90 technical papers, funded research with NASA, Tesla and Joby Aviation, designed two solar-electric vehicles with land speed records.

founders.name: Will Sutton
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder with Doig on the YC launch post; no background given.

investors: US National Science Foundation SBIR Phase I
Australian Government (about 2 million dollars in local currency, 1 million direct and 1 million in kind)

technical_complexity.rationale: Developing novel aerodynamic flow control and a large electric cargo aircraft is research-grade aerospace work; the company built six prototypes of ultra-low-altitude craft before changing technology.

defensibility.rationale: Flow control IP tested with NSF, US Air Force and Australian backing is hard to copy, but the cargo drone market is crowded and unproven at scale.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent move against Seaflight was found. Partners across aerospace are described as interested in incorporating the technology.

market_need_then: The YC launch post argues electric aircraft lacked range and payload and that smaller wings and flow control would remove the green penalty; no dated demand evidence beyond that was found.

identity.mascot_or_character: A flying robot called CC provides autonomy (company site)
identity.voice_and_tone: Confident and playful; the FAQ answers whether it is an aircraft, robotics or logistics company with Yes

branding.brand_signature: CC the flying robot and the line world's most efficient aircraft

brand_strength.rationale: Company site shows personality, but press mostly covers grants. A similarly named Pacific Seaflight wingship company exists, which can confuse searches.

pivots.to: Aerodynamic flow control for electric fixed-wing aircraft and a cargo drone
pivots.why: After six prototypes and several world-first flights the economics did not work, per the YC launch post

outcome_analysis: Seaflight pivoted from ground effect wingships to aerodynamic flow control for electric aircraft, and funds itself through grants from NSF, the US Air Force and the Australian Government. It unveiled a cargo drone in February 2026 and is active. Capital intensity and aerospace certification are the risks; equity funding is only partly known from aggregators.
notes: Unverified aggregator figures: CB Insights lists 3.68 million dollars over seven rounds with the last a 30K convertible note in July 2023, and another listing says 2.9 million; equity investors named by the site and aggregators are Collaborative Fund, Climate Capital, 7 Percent Ventures and Bossa Invest, with no amounts or dates verified, so no equity round is recorded. The NSF grant date and amount come from a search summary that cited CB Insights and employbl as well as the Airframer release. The Australian grant is described as 2 million without a stated currency and as 1.48 million Australian dollars in a Macquarie University headline, so the USD amount is null. No competitor with a source dated near the August 2022 batch was found: the YC launch post names none and the searches returned only undated or later lists (Natilus, Elroy Air, Dronamics), so the list is empty. Founded year per YC page; YC lists Sydney and Torrance, CA.
